title: Precept Six - Non-talking about Others' Errors and Faults
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: The talk's main teaching is about cultivating awareness and compassion for ourselves and others, particularly when it comes to speaking negatively about or judging others. By practicing non-disparaging speech and approaching ourselves with kindness and compassion, we can see beyond our own biases and separateness, and develop a deeper understanding of the interconnected nature of all beings. This practice allows us to let go of our need for protection from others and instead find support in everyone and everything, leading to greater trust and peace.

sentences.text: I want to start with a quote from Dogen, which he always inspires me about practicing with the precepts.
He says, practicing all virtues means getting dirty in order to embrace beings who are mired in the mud.
Getting muddy means admitting your unwholesome tendencies and your own self-obsessions and your own confusion.
Practicing all virtues means getting dirty in order to embrace beings who are mired in the mud.
Getting muddy means admitting your unwholesome tendencies, your own self-obsessions and your own confusion.
This was, indeed, part of our intention throughout the course: to create a safe space where you can explore your unwholesome tendencies, self-obsessions and confusions.

As Nancy Baker says, we've read this over and over in her book, the essence of this practice is to investigate the killer, the liar, the stealer, the greedy one in yourself to really meet that part of yourself and then see what happens in that meeting.

So tonight I'm going to talk about the precept of non-disparaging others and I want to say again, I think this is the most difficult precept for me, although I think you've heard me say that maybe each month when I start my talk because they are all hard, they are actually impossible.
Norman Fischer once said to me, practicing the precepts is like walking towards the horizon, right?
We can practice with them forever.
Let me tell you a little bit about my experience working with this precept.
I grew up in a pretty critical household.
My father was quite harsh, my mother was quite perfectionistic and harsh speech, criticism, condescension was pretty normalized in that family.
As an adult, it became pretty clear to me early on how much I had interjected those modes of communication and I worked really hard.

I have worked really hard throughout my adult life to really be conscious about how I communicate, my choice of words, to be more kind in my speech, to withhold my criticisms or my blame in relationships to other people.
I'm certain that over the years I have softened.
I'm not as sharp edged as I used to be, yet I don't feel any closer to the horizon.
I've been rereading Norman Fischer's book on the Paramitas called *The World Could Be Otherwise* and after each chapter he gives home practices.
After the chapter on the Paramita of ethical conduct, he suggested a home practice of noticing each time you're critical.
I took on this practice trying to notice each time I was critical of myself or others.

And wow, I've been practicing with that in recent weeks and I think at least a hundred or hundreds of times each day critical thoughts pass through my mind: judgments, assessments, accusations, maybe directed towards myself, maybe directed towards others.
While I withhold my critical speech much more than I used to, that I've learned, my critical mind and my attitude is still quite active.
So I continue to walk towards the horizon.
This precept of non-disparaging others includes more than criticism.
It's much more Nancy Baker, maybe if you've had the chance to read the chapter on this, kind of breaks down disparaging others into like four different ways to practice with it.
First is not looking for or finding faults in others, but the second is not speaking about those faults, so not articulating the criticism to them or to another person.
And then the third way she says is not allowing others to speak of faults, so in other words, not participating in their gossip.
That's hard.
And then the fourth way is not expounding on that gossip, in other words, withholding the impulse to repeat it, even if it seems like juicy.
I just think about like when I'm talking with a friend and they are complaining about others in a way that's disparaging, they're actually looking for my support.
So how do I offer support?
How do I commiserate without indulging in their gossip?
I know I often feel the impulse to support their, to support their judgment in an effort to support them.
And then the impulse to share it when someone says, "Well, how so-and-so doing?"
And then I find myself repeating the story.
Other ways to practice with this precept: noticing when you demonize public or political figures.
I think this is pretty familiar to most of us, especially living in this time.
But of course, that just reinforces the "I'm right and they're wrong" perspective, which is a hard one to give up because I am right, right?
And then there's something that Diane Rosetto calls freezing another person.
You have an experience with that person and based on that experience, you draw a conclusion about that person.
That conclusion gets frozen in your mind.
Let's say somebody, I have a date to have tea or coffee with a friend and they stand me up and I conclude in my mind that they're not reliable.
I draw a conclusion about them.
But who knows?
Maybe they are reliable.
Maybe they were just having a bad day because they received disturbing news, maybe at work or in their family about a loved one's health.
Maybe they were just upset that day and preoccupied and yet I've already pinned them: "I can't rely on that person."
So what would it be like to meet someone each time as if it was the first time without bringing with you new, frozen perceptions, assumptions based on past experience?
Harsh speech also of course includes being gruff with someone if you're angry, rough, maybe consciously, maybe unconsciously.
Maybe you don't realize how snappy you're being.
I know that happens for me.
So what are some of the things that motivate harmful speech?
Another question you could ask yourself is, "What's in it for me?
How does it serve me?"
The ego of course is naturally self-serving.
I want to be right.
I want to be seen.
I want to be seen in a positive light.
I want others to like me.
So speaking ill of others may be in service of those ego needs.
Gossiping is self-serving by getting other people to see things my way, to reinforce my "I'm-rightness."
And when we speak of others' faults or we blame them, it's an avoidance of seeing that in ourselves.
It's a way to avoid self-responsibility or being honest with ourselves about our own faults or weaknesses.
What would it be like to include all those things we want to split off or exclude about ourselves from ourselves?
What strikes me about this precept, of course, is that it implies the capacity to accept, to let go of preferences, which we know is not so easy.
So we don't reject or exclude anyone or any part of anyone or any part of yourself.
Another part of this precept is kind of related to freezing others: your perception of others in your mind is to investigate our assumptions about others.
I told you the practice that I took from Norman's book on the Paramitas about noticing when I was critical.
There was another practice I took on, also relating to the chapter he wrote on ethical conduct.
That practice was to notice each time I made assumptions about someone's motives for speech or actions.
When I took on this practice, I saw how continually, like all the time, I'm making assumptions about what's going on for another person, as if I could know.
But really, how can I?
So what would that be like: to hang out in the sphere of not knowing, open and curious?
Again, meeting someone as if you're meeting them for the first time without having a frozen perception, without being closed to who they are or defending what I think I know about them.
Sometimes it's necessary to speak of others' faults.
I've been in management, maybe some of you have, or you've managed employees, and sometimes we need to give honest feedback, communicate about their work performance.
But you know, this of course begs the question: how do we communicate without putting them down?
Even if our speech is quite skillful, sometimes the slightest inflection in our tone of voice can turn that feedback into a put down.
It makes me think of something Chris Burkhart often says: "This is extra," right?
If you're just giving the bare truth without your opinion or judgment, without your narrative, that's what I think she's talking about when she says, "That's extra.
Just this."

In Diane Rosetto's book on the precepts, she reminds us, speaking of the faults of others is harmful, not just to others, but also to ourselves because it reinforces our separateness, the us and them.
If you really work the precept, this precept or any of the precepts ultimately cultivates our awareness of what Thich Nhat Hanh calls interbeing.
This quote from Rebbe Anderson references that.

He says, "When you carefully, kindly and thoroughly inhabit your body of afflictions, willingly accept your massive confused and unwholesome habits of speech and remain upright, the interdependent nature of these obsessions reveals itself."
And this is a gift.
So when you kindly, thoroughly inhabit your body of afflictions—afflictions, right?

All the unwholesome thoughts or impulses, the confusion, the muddiness that Dogen spoke of at the, you know, that I quoted earlier in the talk—when you accept all that and remain upright, what does he mean by remaining upright?
His book on the precepts is called *Being Upright*.
It to me reminds me of Zazen body, right here, fully present, inhabiting your body, embodied presence.
If you accept your confusion and remain upright, the interdependent nature reveals itself.
And this is a gift.
He goes on to say, though, it's very important that this revelation comes through friendly conversation between you and the obsession.
So when you're talking to yourself, when you're noticing your obsessions, your unwholesome impulses, to be kind, to be friendly, not to disparage yourself for having them.
Because if we do, we're just repeating the same pattern, but directing it towards ourselves.

So if we can remain upright in our kindness and in our compassion for ourselves, as we notice, you know, when I was practicing with noticing my critical thoughts, when I was practicing with noticing all the ways I make assumptions about others as I move through my day, and I hold that with compassion for myself, that is what enables some movement, some opening in your process of working with the precepts.

What I hear in Reb's message, like in Dogen's message, is again echoing Nancy Baker, encouraging us to meet the liar, the stealer, the greedy one, the intoxicated one, but to meet them all remaining upright, centered in your Zazen body in the midst of the difficult conversation with yourself as you see yourself.
And then as he said, your interdependent nature reveals itself.
The ultimate meaning of this precept, Reb says, I think of all the precepts, I think of all the precepts when practiced mindfully, brings us back to the fundamental belief in our separateness.
When we live from this belief, we need to protect ourselves from others.
There's an implied lack of trust.
And when we realize the interdependent self, we realize that we are supported by everyone and everything.
So naturally, you can trust.

And when we live from this belief, we need to protect ourselves from others.
There's an implied lack of trust.
And when we realize the interdependent self, we realize that we're supported by everyone and everything.
So naturally, you can trust.
Thank you for listening.
